title: Into the market
hookLine: picture ten: the herder walks into town with open hands, helping (Ox-Herding 10)
tomorrow: who did Marcus Aurelius thank first in his notebook?

lines: A CABIN, OR THE THICK OF IT?
cards: Some days the dream is a cabin with no signal. Other days it's being right in the thick of things, useful. Zen has heroes on both sides.
On one, Hanshan, the poet of Cold Mountain, whose poems describe a life up among the cliffs, far from any road.
On the other, Kuoan's tenth picture: the herder walking into the market, chest bare, feet bare, grinning, with open hands. Two heroes, two directions. Which one is the end of the path?

teach.b: Let the hermit speak first. Hanshan's poems say no road reaches Cold Mountain; up there, among clouds and pines, the world's noise can't touch the mind.
Their best case: you can't give what you haven't found, and finding takes quiet. A guide who has never been alone with their own mind has little to hand anyone.

teach.h: EVEN HANSHAN CAME TO THE KITCHEN.
teach.b: And tradition says even Hanshan came down now and then, to a temple kitchen, where his friend Shide saved him the leftovers. Now the market.
The preface says the herder's gate is shut, and even the wise don't know his inner life. He carries a gourd of wine into the market and leans on his staff on the way home.
In the wine shop and the fish market, everyone he meets wakes up.
The verse: dusty, smeared with ash, smiling wide, no need for the powers of the gods; he simply makes dead trees bloom. Their best case: the whole series was for this.
Awakening that stays on the mountain hasn't finished the circle. Zen honors both.
But Kuoan's ten pictures end in town.
The title of the last one says it: entering the market with open hands.

how: Zen honors both the hermit, like Hanshan, and the teacher who returns to ordinary life; the tenth ox-herding picture shows a smiling figure in the market. People on this path bring their practice back into town as help.

o: the tenth picture: back in town, helping with open hands
the day a herder finally sells his ox at the fair
a monk's begging round through the village at dawn

games.q: the mountain and the market: tap the pairs.

s: in the tenth picture, the herder comes back to town in fine robes
the verse has him bare-chested and barefoot, smeared with dust and ash, smiling wide.
Hanshan's poems describe a life high on Cold Mountain
they say no road reaches it; up there the world's noise can't touch the mind.
in the tenth picture, the herder works wonders with secret powers
the verse says no powers of the gods are needed; dead trees simply bloom.

games.q: your friend says spiritual people belong in the world, helping, and hermits are just escaping. state the hermit's best case.
o: you can't give what you haven't found, and finding takes quiet.
hermits are holier than people with jobs and families.
solitude is just a personality type, nothing to do with the way.
games.why: Hanshan's poems make the case for quiet: no road reaches Cold Mountain. Zen honors that too, though Kuoan's pictures end in the market, and tradition says even Hanshan visited the kitchen.

practice: Bring to mind one person in your town who could use a hand this week: a neighbor with groceries, a coworker, someone at the shop.
Picture the help itself, then the thing most likely to stop you, then what you'll do when that thing shows up.

wordCard.voice: Into the market: Kuoan's tenth picture. Back in town, dusty and smiling, helping with open hands.

orig.note: Chinese: entering the market with hands hanging open, the title of Kuoan's tenth picture.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: open hands, because the pictures end in the market, not on the mountain. All ten, done.

sources.ref: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 10 'Entering the Market with Open Hands' (preface and verse)
